{{Short description|Statistical modeling technique}}
{{Regression bar}}

'''Quantile regression''' is a type of [[regression analysis]] used in statistics and econometrics.  Whereas the [[method of least squares]] estimates the conditional ''[[mean]]'' of the response variable across values of the predictor variables, quantile regression estimates the conditional ''[[median]]'' (or other ''[[quantiles]]'') of the response variable. There is also a method for predicting the conditional [[geometric mean]] of the response variable,<ref name="tofallis2015">Tofallis (2015). "A Better Measure of Relative Prediction Accuracy for Model Selection and Model Estimation", ''Journal of the Operational Research Society'', 66(8):1352-1362. [https://ssrn.com/abstract=2635088]</ref>. Quantile regression is an extension of linear regression used when the conditions of linear regression are not met. It was introduced by [[Roger Koenker]] in 1978. As a complementary and extended approach to the [[Least squares|least squares method]], quantile regression addresses the limitations of least squares method in the presence of heteroscedasticity and ensures the robustness of quantile regression through its robustness to outliers, which compensates for the weakness of least squares method in dealing with outlier data.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Quantile Regression Model and Its Application Research|url=https://drpress.org/ojs/index.php/ajst/article/view/15595|journal=Academic Journal of Science and Technology|date=2023-12-28|issn=2771-3032|pages=172–176|volume=8|issue=3|doi=10.54097/vt1qpm59|first=Mengfan|last=Xu|doi-access=free}}</ref> 
[[File:Quantilsregression.svg|thumb|Example for quantile regression]]

==Advantages and applications==

One advantage of quantile regression relative to ordinary least squares regression is that the quantile regression estimates are more robust against outliers in the response measurements. However, the main attraction of quantile regression goes beyond this and is advantageous when conditional quantile functions are of interest.  Different measures of [[central tendency]] and [[statistical dispersion]] can be used to more comprehensively analyze the relationship between variables.<ref name="Koenker2005">{{cite book|title=Quantile Regression|url=https://archive.org/details/quantileregressi00koen_757|url-access=limited|last=Koenker|first=Roger|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2005|isbn=978-0-521-60827-5|pages=[https://archive.org/details/quantileregressi00koen_757/page/n151 146]–7}}</ref>

In [[ecology]], quantile regression has been proposed and used as a way to discover more useful predictive relationships between variables in cases where there is no relationship or only a weak relationship between the means of such variables.  The need for and success of quantile regression in ecology has been attributed to the [[complexity]] of interactions between different factors leading to [[data]] with unequal variation of one variable for different ranges of another variable.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Brian S. |last1=Cade |first2=Barry R. |last2=Noon |year=2003 |url=http://www.econ.uiuc.edu/~roger/research/rq/QReco.pdf |title=A gentle introduction to quantile regression for ecologists |journal=Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment |volume=1 |issue=8 |pages=412–420 |doi= 10.2307/3868138|jstor=3868138 }}</ref>

Another application of quantile regression is in the areas of growth charts, where percentile curves are commonly used to screen for abnormal growth.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wei |first1=Y. |last2=Pere |first2=A. |last3=Koenker |first3=R. |last4=He |first4=X. |year=2006 |title=Quantile Regression Methods for Reference Growth Charts |journal=[[Statistics in Medicine (journal)|Statistics in Medicine]] |volume=25 |issue=8 |pages=1369–1382 |doi=10.1002/sim.2271 |pmid=16143984 |s2cid=7830193 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wei |first1=Y. |last2=He |first2=X.|author2-link=Xuming He |year=2006 |title=Conditional Growth Charts (with discussions) |journal=[[Annals of Statistics]] |volume=34 |issue=5 |pages=2069–2097 and 2126–2131 |doi=10.1214/009053606000000623 |arxiv=math/0702634 |s2cid=88516697 }}</ref>

==History==
The idea of estimating a median regression slope, a major theorem about minimizing sum of the absolute deviances and a geometrical algorithm for constructing median regression was proposed in 1760 by [[Roger Joseph Boscovich|Ruđer Josip Bošković]], a [[Society of Jesus|Jesuit Catholic]] priest from Dubrovnik.<ref name="Koenker2005" />{{rp|4}}<ref>{{cite journal |last=Stigler |first=S. |year=1984 |title=Boscovich, Simpson and a 1760 manuscript note on fitting a linear relation |journal=Biometrika |volume=71 |issue=3 |pages=615–620 |doi=10.1093/biomet/71.3.615 }}</ref> He was interested in the ellipticity of the earth, building on Isaac Newton's suggestion that its rotation could cause it to bulge at the [[equator]] with a corresponding flattening at the poles.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Quantile Regression|url=https://archive.org/details/quantileregressi00koen_757|url-access=limited|last=Koenker|first=Roger|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2005|isbn=9780521845731|location=Cambridge|pages=[https://archive.org/details/quantileregressi00koen_757/page/n7 2]}}</ref> He finally produced the first geometric procedure for determining the [[equator]] of a rotating [[planet]] from three [[observation]]s of a surface feature. More importantly for quantile regression, he was able to develop the first evidence of the least absolute criterion and preceded the least squares introduced by [[Legendre polynomials|Legendre]] in 1805 by fifty years.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Quantile Regression: Estimation and Simulation|last1=Furno|first1=Marilena|last2=Vistocco|first2=Domenico|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|year=2018|isbn=9781119975281|location=Hoboken, NJ|pages=xv}}</ref>

Other thinkers began building upon Bošković's idea such as [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]], who developed the so-called "methode de situation." This led to [[Francis Ysidro Edgeworth|Francis Edgeworth]]'s plural median<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.econ.uiuc.edu/~roger/research/galton/Galton.pdf|title=Galton, Edgeworth, Frisch, and prospects for quantile regression in economics|last=Koenker|first=Roger|date=August 1998|website=UIUC.edu|access-date=August 22, 2018}}</ref> - a geometric approach to median regression - and is recognized as the precursor of the [[Simplex algorithm|simplex method]].<ref name=":0" /> The works of Bošković, Laplace, and Edgeworth were recognized as a prelude to [[Roger Koenker]]'s contributions to quantile regression.

Median regression computations for larger data sets are quite tedious compared to the least squares method, for which reason it has historically generated a lack of popularity among statisticians, until the widespread adoption of computers in the latter part of the 20th century.

==Background: quantiles==
Quantile regression expresses the conditional quantiles of a dependent variable as a linear function of the explanatory variables. Crucial to the practicality of quantile regression is that the quantiles can be expressed as the solution of a minimization problem, as we will show in this section before discussing conditional quantiles in the next section.

===Quantile of a random variable===
{{Main|Quantile function}}
Let <math>Y</math> be a real-valued random variable with [[cumulative distribution function]] <math>F_{Y}(y)=P(Y\leq y)</math>. The <math>\tau</math>th quantile of Y is defined as
:<math>q_{Y}(\tau):=F_{Y}^{-1}(\tau):=\inf\left\{ y:F_{Y}(y)\geq\tau\right\},</math>
where <math> 0 < \tau < 1</math>.

Define the [[loss function]] as 
:<math>\rho_{\tau}(u) = u (\tau - \mathbb{I}_{(u < 0)}) =
\begin{cases}
(\tau - 1) u, & \text{if } u < 0, \\
\tau u, & \text{if } u \geq 0, 
\end{cases}</math>
where <math> 0 < \tau < 1</math>, <math>\mathbb{I}(\cdot)</math> is an [[indicator function]]. 
It is observed that <math>\tau > (1-\tau)</math> for <math>\tau > 0.5</math>, and <math>\tau < (1-\tau)</math> for <math>\tau < 0.5</math>. The intuition is that for higher quantiles (<math>\tau > 0.5</math>), we penalize the positive residuals more than negative residuals, and vice versa, and the loss is unsymmetric. However, for <math>\tau = 0.5</math> the penalization is symmetric (hence, this results in a median estimator). 
A specific quantile can be found by minimizing the expected loss of <math>Y-u</math> with respect to <math>u</math>:<ref name="Koenker2005" />({{pp.|5|6}}):

:<math>
\begin{array}{lll}
q_{Y}(\tau) &=& \underset{u}{\mbox{arg min}} \mathbb{E}(\rho_{\tau}(Y-u)) \\
&=& \underset{u}{\mbox{arg min}} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \rho_{\tau}(y-u) dF_{Y}(y) \\
&=& \underset{u}{\mbox{arg min}}\biggl\{(\tau-1)\int_{-\infty}^{u}(y-u)dF_{Y}(y)+\tau\int_{u}^{\infty}(y-u)dF_{Y}(y)\biggr\}.
\end{array}
</math>

This can be shown by computing the derivative of the expected loss with respect to <math>u</math> via an application of the [[Leibniz integral rule]], setting it to 0, and letting <math>q_{\tau}</math> be the solution of
:<math>0=(1-\tau)\int_{-\infty}^{q_{\tau}}dF_{Y}(y)-\tau\int_{q_{\tau}}^{\infty}dF_{Y}(y).</math>
This equation reduces to
:<math>0=F_{Y}(q_{\tau})-\tau,</math>
and then to
:<math>F_{Y}(q_{\tau})=\tau.</math>
If the solution <math>q_{\tau}</math> is not unique, then we have to take the infimum of all such solutions to obtain
the <math>\tau</math>th quantile of the random variable ''Y''.

====Example====
Let <math>Y</math> be a discrete random variable that takes values <math>y_i = i</math> with <math>i = 1,2,\dots,9</math> with equal probabilities. The task is to find the median of Y, and hence the value <math>\tau=0.5</math> is chosen. Then the expected loss of <math>Y-u</math> is
:<math>
\begin{array}{lll}
L(u) &=& E(\rho_{\tau}(Y-u))=\frac{(\tau-1)}{9}\sum_{y_{i}<u}(y_{i}-u)+\frac{\tau}{9}\sum_{y_{i}\geq u}(y_{i}-u) \\
&=& \frac{0.5}{9}\Bigl(-\sum_{y_{i}<u}(y_{i}-u)+\sum_{y_{i}\geq u}(y_{i}-u)\Bigr).
\end{array}
</math>
Since <math>{0.5/9}</math> is a constant, it can be taken out of the expected loss function (this is only true if <math>\tau=0.5</math>). Then, at ''u''=3,
:<math>L(3) \propto\sum_{i=1}^{2}</math><math>-(i-3)</math><math>+\sum_{i=3}^{9}</math><math>(i-3)</math><math> =[(2+1)+(0+1+2+...+6)] =24.</math>

Suppose that ''u'' is increased by 1 unit. Then the expected loss will be changed by <math>(3)-(6)=-3</math> on changing ''u'' to 4. If,  ''u''=5, the expected loss is
:<math>L(5) \propto \sum_{i=1}^{4}i+\sum_{i=0}^{4}i=20,</math>
and any change in ''u'' will increase the expected loss. Thus ''u''=5 is the median. The table below shows the expected loss (divided by <math>{0.5/9}</math>) for different values of ''u''.

{| class="wikitable"
|-
| ''u'' || 1|| 2|| 3|| 4|| 5|| 6|| 7|| 8|| 9
|-
| Expected loss||36|| 29|| 24|| 21|| 20|| 21|| 24|| 29 || 36
|}

====Intuition====
Consider <math>\tau=0.5</math> and let ''q'' be an initial guess for <math>q_{\tau}</math>. The expected loss evaluated at ''q'' is
:<math>L(q)=-0.5\int_{-\infty}^{q}(y-q)dF_{Y}(y)+0.5\int_{q}^{\infty}(y-q)dF_{Y}(y) .</math>
In order to minimize the expected loss, we move the value of ''q'' a little bit to see whether the expected loss will rise or fall.
Suppose we increase ''q'' by 1 unit. Then the change of expected loss would be
:<math>\int_{-\infty}^{q}1dF_{Y}(y)-\int_{q}^{\infty}1dF_{Y}(y) .</math>

The first term of the equation is <math>F_{Y}(q)</math> and second term of the equation is <math>1-F_{Y}(q)</math>. Therefore, the change of expected loss function is negative if and only if <math>F_{Y}(q)<0.5</math>, that is if and only if ''q'' is smaller than the median. Similarly, if we reduce ''q'' by 1 unit, the change of expected loss function is negative if and only if ''q'' is larger than the median.

In order to minimize the expected loss function, we would increase (decrease) ''q'' if ''q'' is smaller (larger) than the median, until ''q'' reaches the median. The idea behind the minimization is to count the number of points (weighted with the density) that are larger or smaller than ''q'' and then move ''q'' to a point where ''q'' is larger than <math>100\tau</math>% of the points.

===Sample quantile===
The <math>\tau</math> sample quantile can be obtained by using an [[importance sampling]] estimate and solving the following minimization problem

:<math>\hat{q}_{\tau}=\underset{q\in \mathbb{R}}{\mbox{arg min}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\rho_{\tau}(y_{i}-q) ,</math>
:<math>=\underset{q\in \mathbb{R}}{\mbox{arg min}}  \left[(\tau-1)\sum_{y_{i}<q}(y_{i}-q)+\tau\sum_{y_{i}\geq q}(y_{i}-q) \right]</math>, 
where the function <math>\rho_{\tau}</math> is the tilted absolute value function. The intuition is the same as for the population quantile.

==Conditional quantile and quantile regression==
The <math>\tau</math>th conditional quantile of <math>Y</math> given <math>X</math> is the <math>\tau</math>th quantile of the
[[Conditional probability distribution]] of <math>Y</math> given <math>X</math>,
:<math>Q_{Y|X}(\tau)=\inf\left\{ y:F_{Y|X}(y)\geq\tau\right\}</math>.
We use a capital <math>Q</math> to denote the conditional quantile to indicate that it is a random variable.

In quantile regression for the <math>\tau</math>th quantile we make the assumption that the <math>\tau</math>th conditional quantile is given as a linear function of the explanatory variables:
:<math> Q_{Y|X}(\tau)=X\beta_{\tau}</math>. 
Given the distribution function of <math>Y</math>,  <math>\beta_{\tau}</math> can be obtained by solving
:<math>\beta_{\tau}=\underset{\beta\in \mathbb{R}^{k}}{\mbox{arg min}}E(\rho_{\tau}(Y-X\beta)).</math>

Solving the sample analog gives the estimator of <math>\beta</math>.
:<math>\hat{\beta_{\tau}}=\underset{\beta\in \mathbb{R}^{k}}{\mbox{arg min}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\rho_{\tau}(Y_{i}-X_{i}\beta)) .</math>

Note that when <math>\tau = 0.5</math>, the loss function <math>\rho_\tau</math> is proportional to the absolute value function, and thus median regression is the same as 
linear regression by [[least absolute deviations]].

==Computation of estimates for regression parameters==
The mathematical forms arising from quantile regression are distinct from those arising in the [[method of least squares]].  The method of least squares leads to a consideration of problems in an [[inner product space]], involving [[projection (mathematics)|projection]] onto subspaces, and thus the problem of minimizing the squared errors can be reduced to a problem in [[numerical linear algebra]]. Quantile regression does not have this structure, and instead the minimization problem can be reformulated as a [[linear programming]] problem
:<math>\underset{\beta,u^{+},u^{-}\in \mathbb{R}^{k}\times \mathbb{R}_{+}^{2n}}{\min}\left\{ \tau1_{n}^{'}u^{+}+(1-\tau)1_{n}^{'}u^{-}|X\beta+u^{+}-u^{-}=Y\right\} ,</math>

where
:<math>u_{j}^{+}=\max(u_{j},0)</math> ,&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <math>u_{j}^{-}=-\min(u_{j},0).</math>

[[Simplex algorithm|Simplex methods]]<ref name="Koenker2005" />{{rp|181}}  or [[interior point method]]s<ref name="Koenker2005" />{{rp|190}} can be applied to solve the linear programming problem.

==Asymptotic properties==

For <math>\tau\in(0,1)</math>, under some regularity conditions, <math>\hat{\beta}_{\tau}</math> is [[Asymptotic normality|asymptotically normal]]:
:<math>\sqrt{n}(\hat{\beta}_{\tau}-\beta_{\tau})\overset{d}{\rightarrow}N(0,\tau(1-\tau)D^{-1}\Omega_{x}D^{-1}),</math>
where
:<math>D=E(f_{Y}(X\beta)XX^{\prime})</math> and <math>\Omega_{x}=E(X^{\prime} X) .</math>

Direct estimation of the asymptotic variance-covariance matrix is not always satisfactory. Inference for quantile regression parameters can be made with the regression rank-score tests or with the bootstrap methods.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kocherginsky |first1=M. |last2=He |first2=X. |last3=Mu |first3=Y. |year=2005 |title=Practical Confidence Intervals for Regression Quantiles |journal=[[Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics]] |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=41–55 |doi=10.1198/106186005X27563 |s2cid=120598656 }}</ref>

==Equivariance==

See [[invariant estimator]] for background on invariance or see [[equivariance]].

===Scale equivariance===

For any <math>a>0</math> and <math>\tau\in[0,1]</math>
:<math>\hat{\beta}(\tau;aY,X)=a\hat{\beta}(\tau;Y,X),</math>
:<math>\hat{\beta}(\tau;-aY,X)=-a\hat{\beta}(1-\tau;Y,X).</math>

===Shift equivariance===
For any <math>\gamma\in R^{k}</math> and <math>\tau\in[0,1]</math>
:<math>\hat{\beta}(\tau;Y+X\gamma,X)=\hat{\beta}(\tau;Y,X)+\gamma .</math>

===Equivariance to reparameterization of design===
Let <math>A</math> be any <math>p\times p</math> nonsingular matrix and <math>\tau\in[0,1] </math>
:<math>\hat{\beta}(\tau;Y,XA)=A^{-1}\hat{\beta}(\tau;Y,X) .</math>

===Invariance to monotone transformations===
If <math>h</math> is a nondecreasing function on <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, the following [[Invariant estimator|invariance]] property applies:

:<math>h(Q_{Y|X}(\tau))\equiv Q_{h(Y)|X}(\tau).</math>

Example (1):

If <math>W=\exp(Y)</math> and <math>Q_{Y|X}(\tau)=X\beta_{\tau}</math>, then <math>Q_{W|X}(\tau)=\exp(X\beta_{\tau})</math>. The mean regression does not have the same property since <math>\operatorname{E} (\ln(Y))\neq \ln(\operatorname{E}(Y)).</math>

== Inference ==

=== Interpretation of the slope parameters ===

The linear model  <math> Q_{Y|X}(\tau)=X\beta_{\tau}</math> mis-specifies the true systematic relation <math> Q_{Y|X}(\tau)=f(X,\tau)</math>  when <math> f(\cdot,\tau)</math> is nonlinear. However, <math> Q_{Y|X}(\tau)=X\beta_{\tau}</math> minimizes a weighted distanced to <math> f(X,\tau)</math> among linear models.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Angrist |first1=J. |last2=Chernozhukov |first2=V. | last3=Fernandez-Val |first3=I.| year=2006 |title=Quantile Regression under Misspecification, with an Application to the U.S. Wage Structure |journal=[[Econometrica]] |volume=74 |issue=2 |pages=539–563 |doi=10.1111/j.1468-0262.2006.00671.x |url=http://papers.nber.org/papers/w10428.pdf }}</ref> Furthermore, the slope parameters <math> \beta_{\tau}</math> of the linear model can be interpreted as weighted averages of the derivatives <math> \nabla f(X,\tau)</math> so that <math> \beta_{\tau}</math> can be used for causal inference.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kato |first1=R. |last2=Sasaki |first2=Y. | year=2017 |title=On Using Linear Quantile Regressions for Causal Inference |journal=[[Econometric Theory]] |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=664–690 |doi=10.1017/S0266466616000177 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Specifically, the hypothesis <math> H_0: \nabla f(x,\tau)=0</math> for all <math> x</math> implies the hypothesis <math> H_0: \beta_\tau=0</math>, which can be tested using the estimator <math>\hat{\beta_{\tau}}</math> and its limit distribution.

=== Goodness of fit ===
The [[goodness of fit]] for quantile regression for the <math>\tau</math> quantile can be defined as:<ref>Roger Koenker & José A. F. Machado (1999) Goodness of Fit and Related Inference Processes for Quantile Regression, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 94:448, 1296-1310, DOI: 10.1080/01621459.1999.10473882
</ref>
<math>R^1(\tau)=1-\frac{\hat{V}_\tau}{\tilde{V}_\tau},</math>
where <math>\hat{V}_\tau</math> is the minimized expected loss function under the full model, while <math>\tilde{V}_\tau</math> is the expected loss function under the intercept-only model.

==Variants==

=== Bayesian methods for quantile regression ===

Because quantile regression does not normally assume a parametric likelihood for the conditional distributions of Y|X, the Bayesian methods work with a working likelihood. A convenient choice is the asymmetric Laplacian likelihood,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kozumi |first1=H. |last2=Kobayashi |first2=G. |year=2011 |title=Gibbs sampling methods for Bayesian quantile regression |journal=[[Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation]] |volume=81 |issue=11 |pages=1565–1578 |doi=10.1080/00949655.2010.496117 |s2cid=44015988 |url=https://www.b.kobe-u.ac.jp/papers_files/2009_02.pdf }}</ref> because the mode of the resulting posterior under a flat prior is the usual quantile regression estimates. The posterior inference, however, must be interpreted with care.  Yang, Wang and He<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Y. |last2=Wang |first2=H.X. | last3=He |first3=X.| year=2016 |title=Posterior Inference in Bayesian Quantile Regression with Asymmetric Laplace Likelihood |journal=[[International Statistical Review]] |volume=84 |issue=3 |pages=327–344 |doi=10.1111/insr.12114 |hdl=2027.42/135059 |s2cid=14947362 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> provided a posterior variance adjustment for valid inference. In addition,
Yang and He<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Y. |last2=He |first2=X. |year=2010 |title=Bayesian empirical likelihood for quantile regression |journal=[[Annals of Statistics]] |volume=40 |issue=2 |pages=1102–1131 |doi=10.1214/12-AOS1005 |arxiv=1207.5378 |s2cid=88519086 }}</ref> showed that one can have asymptotically valid posterior inference if the working likelihood is chosen to be the empirical likelihood.

===Machine learning methods for quantile regression===
Beyond [[simple linear regression]], there are several machine learning methods that can be extended to quantile regression. A switch from the squared error to the tilted absolute value loss function (a.k.a. the ''pinball loss''<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Steinwart | first1 = Ingo | last2 = Christmann | first2 = Andreas | title = Estimating conditional quantiles with the help of the pinball loss | journal = Bernoulli | volume = 17 | issue = 1 | pages = 211–225  | year = 2011  | publisher = Bernoulli Society for Mathematical Statistics and Probability | doi = 10.3150/10-BEJ267 | url = https://doi.org/10.3150/10-BEJ267| arxiv = 1102.2101 }}</ref>) allows gradient descent-based learning algorithms to learn a specified quantile instead of the mean. It means that we can apply all [[neural network]] and [[deep learning]] algorithms to quantile regression,<ref>{{cite arXiv | last=Petneházi | first=Gábor | title=QCNN: Quantile Convolutional Neural Network | date=2019-08-21 | eprint=1908.07978 | class=cs.LG }}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv | last1=Rodrigues | first1=Filipe | last2=Pereira | first2=Francisco C. | title=Beyond expectation: Deep joint mean and quantile regression for spatio-temporal problems | date=2018-08-27 | eprint=1808.08798 | class=stat }}</ref> which is then referred to as [[Nonparametric regression|nonparametric]] quantile regression.<ref>Nonparametric Quantile Regression: Non-Crossing Constraints and Conformal Prediction by Wenlu Tang, Guohao Shen, Yuanyuan Lin, Jian Huang, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.10161.pdf</ref>
Tree-based learning algorithms are also available for quantile regression (see, e.g., Quantile Regression Forests,<ref>{{cite journal | last=Meinshausen | first=Nicolai | title=Quantile Regression Forests | url=http://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume7/meinshausen06a/meinshausen06a.pdf | journal=Journal of Machine Learning Research | volume=7 | issue=6 | pages=983–999 | year=2006 }}</ref> as a simple generalization of [[Random forest|Random Forests]]).

===Censored quantile regression===

If the response variable is subject to [[Censoring_(statistics)|censoring]], the conditional mean is not identifiable without additional distributional assumptions, but the conditional quantile is often identifiable. For recent work on censored quantile regression, see: Portnoy<ref name="Portnoy2003">{{cite journal |last=Portnoy |first=S. L. |year=2003 |title=Censored Regression Quantiles |journal=[[Journal of the American Statistical Association]] |volume=98 |issue=464 |pages=1001–1012 |doi=10.1198/016214503000000954 |s2cid=120674851 }}</ref>
and Wang and Wang<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=H. |author1-link= Huixia Judy Wang |last2=Wang |first2=L. |year=2009 |title=Locally Weighted Censored Quantile Regression |journal=[[Journal of the American Statistical Association]] |volume=104 |issue=487 |pages=1117–1128 |doi=10.1198/jasa.2009.tm08230 |citeseerx=10.1.1.504.796 |s2cid=34494316 }}</ref>

Example (2):

Let <math>Y^{c}=\max(0,Y)</math> and <math>Q_{Y|X}=X\beta_{\tau}</math>. Then <math>Q_{Y^{c}|X}(\tau)=\max(0,X\beta_{\tau})</math>. This is the censored quantile regression model: estimated values can be obtained without making any distributional assumptions, but at the cost of computational difficulty,<ref>{{cite journal |first=James L. |last=Powell |year=1986 |title=Censored Regression Quantiles |journal=[[Journal of Econometrics]] |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=143–155 |doi=10.1016/0304-4076(86)90016-3 }}</ref> some of which can be avoided by using a simple three step censored quantile regression procedure as an approximation.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Victor |last1=Chernozhukov |first2=Han |last2=Hong |title=Three-Step Censored Quantile Regression and Extramarital Affairs |journal=[[Journal of the American Statistical Association|J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.]] |volume=97 |issue=459 |pages=872–882 |year=2002 |doi=10.1198/016214502388618663 |s2cid=1410755 }}</ref>

For random censoring on the response variables, the censored quantile regression of Portnoy (2003)<ref name="Portnoy2003" /> provides consistent estimates of all identifiable quantile functions based on reweighting each censored point appropriately.

Censored quantile regression has close links to [[survival analysis]].
[[File:Km plot.jpg|thumb|250px|Depiction of two [[Kaplan–Meier estimator]]s for the survival probabilities <math>S(t)=1-F(t)</math> of two patient groups as a function of time <math>t</math>, where <math>F(t)</math> is the distribution function of the deaths. The <math>\tau</math> quantile of the deaths is <math>t_\tau = F^{-1}(\tau)</math>, where <math>F^{-1}</math> is the [[quantile function]] of the deaths. Censored quantile regression can be used to estimate these conditional quantiles individually, while survival analysis estimates the (conditional) survival function.]]

=== Heteroscedastic errors ===
The quantile regression loss needs to be adapted in the presence of heteroscedastic errors in order to be [[Efficiency (statistics)|efficient]].<ref>Efficient Quantile Regression for Heteroscedastic
Models by, Yoonsuh Jung, Yoonkyung Lee, Steven N. MacEachern, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00949655.2014.967244?journalCode=gscs20</ref>

==Implementations==
Numerous statistical software packages include implementations of quantile regression:
* [[MATLAB|Matlab]] function <code>quantreg</code><ref>{{Cite web|title = quantreg(x,y,tau,order,Nboot) - File Exchange - MATLAB Central|url = http://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/32115-quantreg-x-y-tau-order-nboot-|website = www.mathworks.com|access-date = 2016-02-01|archive-date = 2016-03-12|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160312064420/http://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/32115-quantreg-x-y-tau-order-nboot-|url-status = dead}}</ref>
* [[gretl]] has the <code>quantreg</code> command.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Gretl Command Reference|url = http://ricardo.ecn.wfu.edu/pub//gretl/manual/en/gretl-ref.pdf|date = April 2017|access-date = 2017-04-22|archive-date = 2018-12-15|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20181215121225/http://ricardo.ecn.wfu.edu/pub//gretl/manual/en/gretl-ref.pdf|url-status = dead}}</ref>
* [[R (programming language)|R]] offers several packages that implement quantile regression, most notably <code>quantreg</code> by [[Roger Koenker]],<ref>{{cite web |title=quantreg: Quantile Regression |work=R Project |date= 2018-12-18|url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/quantreg/index.html }}</ref> but also <code>gbm</code>,<ref>{{cite web |title=gbm: Generalized Boosted Regression Models |work=R Project |date= 2019-01-14|url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/gbm/ }}</ref> <code>quantregForest</code>,<ref>{{cite web |title=quantregForest: Quantile Regression Forests |work=R Project |date= 2017-12-19|url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/quantregForest/index.html }}</ref> <code>qrnn</code><ref>{{cite web |title=qrnn: Quantile Regression Neural Networks |work=R Project |date= 2018-06-26|url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/qrnn/index.html }}</ref> and <code>qgam</code><ref>{{cite web |title=qgam: Smooth Additive Quantile Regression Models |work=R Project |date= 2019-05-23|url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/qgam/index.html }}</ref>
* [[Python (programming language)|Python]], via <code>Scikit-garden</code><ref>{{cite web |title=Quantile Regression Forests |url=https://scikit-garden.github.io/examples/QuantileRegressionForests/ |website=Scikit-garden |access-date=3 January 2019}}</ref> and <code>statsmodels</code><ref>{{cite web |title=Statsmodels: Quantile Regression |url=https://www.statsmodels.org/dev/examples/notebooks/generated/quantile_regression.html |website=Statsmodels |access-date=15 November 2019}}</ref>; dedicated package <code>Regressionizer</code><ref>{{cite web |title= Regressionizer |url=https://pypi.org/project/Regressionizer/ |website=PyPI.org |access-date=17 February 2026}}</ref>.
* [[SAS System|SAS]] through <code>proc quantreg</code> (ver. 9.2)<ref>{{cite web |title=An Introduction to Quantile Regression and the QUANTREG Procedure |work=SAS Support |url=http://www2.sas.com/proceedings/sugi30/213-30.pdf }}</ref> and <code>proc quantselect</code> (ver. 9.3).<ref>{{cite web |title=The QUANTSELECT Procedure |work=SAS Support |url=https://support.sas.com/rnd/app/stat/procedures/quantselect.html |access-date=2022-01-12 |archive-date=2022-01-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220112210028/https://support.sas.com/rnd/app/stat/procedures/quantselect.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* [[Stata]], via the <code>qreg</code> command.<ref>{{cite web |title=qreg — Quantile regression |work=Stata Manual |url=https://www.stata.com/manuals15/rqreg.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first1=A. Colin |last1=Cameron |first2=Pravin K. |last2=Trivedi |title=Microeconometrics Using Stata |location=College Station |publisher=Stata Press |edition=Revised |year=2010 |isbn=978-1-59718-073-3 |chapter=Quantile Regression |pages=211–234 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UkKQRAAACAAJ&pg=PA211 }}</ref>
* [[Vowpal Wabbit]], via <code>--loss_function quantile</code>.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/JohnLangford/vowpal_wabbit/wiki/Loss-functions|title=JohnLangford/vowpal_wabbit|website=GitHub|access-date=2016-07-09}}</ref>
* [[Mathematica]] package <code>QuantileRegression.m</code><ref>{{cite web |title=QuantileRegression.m |url=https://github.com/antononcube/MathematicaForPrediction/blob/master/QuantileRegression.m |website=MathematicaForPrediction |access-date=3 January 2019}}</ref> hosted at the MathematicaForPrediction project at GitHub.
* [[Wolfram Language]] function <code>QuantileRegression</code><ref>{{cite web |title=QuantileRegression |url=https://resources.wolframcloud.com/FunctionRepository/resources/QuantileRegression |website=Wolfram Function Repository |access-date=17 February 2026}}</ref> hosted at Wolfram Function Repository. Package (paclet) <code>MonadicQuantileRegression </code><ref>{{cite web |title= MonadicQuantileRegression |url=https://resources.wolframcloud.com/PacletRepository/resources/AntonAntonov/MonadicQuantileRegression |website=Wolfram Language Paclet Repository |access-date=17 February 2026}}</ref> hosted at Wolfram Language Paclet Repository.
